cards.title: Carry ΔT's percentage uncertainty through to ΔH

walkthrough.question:
Iron powder (3.26 g) is stirred into 80.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ copper(II) sulfate solution in a calorimeter:
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
The solution warms by at most 7.5 °C, which gives ΔH = −1.6 × 10² kJ for the reaction as written.
The temperature rise has an uncertainty of ±0.2 °C. Treat this as the only significant uncertainty.
Calculate the absolute uncertainty in ΔH.
walkthrough.key_idea: ΔH is proportional to ΔT, so apply ΔT's percentage uncertainty to ΔH.
walkthrough.question_type: Uncertainty: propagate ΔT through to ΔH
walkthrough.careful: Multiply the percentage by ΔH; stopping at the percentage loses a mark.
procedure: Find the absolute uncertainty in the temperature change.
Divide it by the temperature change itself.
Take other quantities as exact unless uncertainties are given.
Multiply this fraction by the size of ΔH.
State the result as ± with ΔH's units.
tricks: Same % on ΔT and ΔH; fails if mass or moles also carry uncertainty.
Size check: small percentage on ΔT means ± is a small part of ΔH.
if_lost: Which measured quantity has an uncertainty stated in the question?
Does the question want a percentage or an absolute uncertainty?
If ΔT were doubled, what would happen to ΔH?
Once you have a percentage, which value do you apply it to?

1_context.short: Practical skill: ΔT's percentage uncertainty carries through to ΔH.
1_context.why: ΔH comes from mcΔT divided by moles, so any doubt in ΔT scales directly into ΔH. That link makes this a data-processing step, not a new formula.
1_context.avoid: Treating the uncertainty as a separate calculation unrelated to the ΔH already found.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.4: enthalpy change is determined from a temperature change by applying Q = mcΔT and ΔH = −Q/n.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach Q = mcΔT as giving one answer. This question asks how far that answer can be trusted, using one stated uncertainty.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One mark for ΔT's percentage; one for applying it to ΔH.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The two ticks separate finding the relative uncertainty from using it. Examiners report many candidates stopped at the first, so the second tick is where marks go.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at 0.2/7.5: 18N.2.HL.TZ0.1 examiners report many found it, then never multiplied by their molar enthalpy.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The percentage alone earns one mark. The second mark needs the absolute ± value on ΔH.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: 3% or 0.03 stated only. Full: that fraction multiplied by ΔH, giving ±5 kJ.

3_novel_application.short: Same proportional step works whichever reaction or calorimeter appears.
3_novel_application.why: Only the numbers change: any ΔH computed from mcΔT scales with ΔT. The step holds for combustion, neutralisation or displacement when ΔT carries the only stated uncertainty.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using the 3.26 g of iron, the volume or the concentration; no uncertainty is stated for them.
3_novel_application.disguise: It sits inside a displacement and limiting-reagent question, so it looks like more stoichiometry rather than an uncertainty step.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: which measured value carries the ±, and is ΔH proportional to it? If yes, copy its percentage over.

4_command_terms.short: Calculate: show both the percentage and the absolute value.
4_command_terms.why: Calculate means a numerical answer with stages shown. With two separate marks, a visible percentage can earn its own mark even if the final multiplication goes wrong.
4_command_terms.avoid: Giving only a final figure: a wrong one with no working leaves nothing to credit.
4_command_terms.demands: A numerical absolute uncertainty in ΔH with the percentage step visible. The original part's wording is not in the pack; Calculate is this card's wording.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 2 marks, one per step: the percentage or fraction for ΔT, then that fraction times ΔH. Not all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two lines of working: percentage, then multiply.
5_time_efficiency.why: With ΔH already found, this needs one division and one multiplication. Recalculating ΔH at both ends of the temperature range reaches a similar result far more slowly.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Reworking mcΔT at 7.7 °C and 7.3 °C; the proportional step is quicker.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the iron mass and the moles: ΔH is already given, and they add nothing to this step.

6_data_booklet.short: Booklet gives Q = mcΔT; uncertainty rules are not in it.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 1 shows ΔT as a direct factor in Q, which justifies the proportional step. Nothing in the sections provided tells you how to combine uncertainties.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting the booklet for an uncertainty formula: the sections provided here give none.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Read Q = mcΔT in section 1: ΔT is a single multiplying factor, so Q and ΔH scale with it.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ value × 100, and ΔH = −Q/n. Neither is in the booklet sections provided.

7_elimination.short: Rule out any answer that is not a small ± in kJ.
7_elimination.why: Absolute uncertainty shares ΔH's units and, with a small percentage on ΔT, must be a small fraction of ΔH. Checking that rules out these answers without arithmetic.
7_elimination.avoid: Writing ±0.2 kJ by transferring the temperature figure directly onto the enthalpy.

definitely_wrong.target: A bare percentage as the final answer
definitely_wrong.rule: An absolute uncertainty in ΔH must be an energy value, not a percentage.
This copies the temperature uncertainty into energy units; °C and kJ are different scales.

definitely_wrong.target: A ± value close to or larger than ΔH
definitely_wrong.rule: The uncertainty is a small part of ΔT, so it must be a small part of ΔH.

walkthrough.answer: 0.2/7.5 × 100 = 3% (0.03), then 0.03 × 160 kJ = ±5 kJ. The markscheme rounds to 3% before multiplying. Unrounded, 2.67% gives about ±4.3 kJ, and the pack shows only the rounded route.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.4: ΔH is determined from a temperature change using Q = mcΔT and ΔH = −Q/n.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stop at a single ΔH value. Exams go on to ask how much a stated uncertainty in ΔT affects that value.

trigger_phrases: Apply it to ΔH: 0.03 × 160 kJ = ±5 kJ
trap_boundaries: Stopping at the percentage earns one of the two marks (18N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
The fraction is taken over the temperature change, not over a single temperature reading (25N.1B.HL.6220.2).
25N.1B.HL.6220.2 accepts 20% and answers in the range 15–18% for a value read from the candidate's graph.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit finds ΔT's percentage uncertainty. Full credit also multiplies that fraction by ΔH to give an absolute ± value.

disguises: A final part of a displacement and limiting-reagent question.
A ΔT read from a graph's intersecting lines in a thermometric experiment, with a ± read from that graph.
Different names for the same thing: relative, percentage or fractional uncertainty.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find the quantity with the ±, check that ΔH is directly proportional to it, then carry its percentage straight across.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Two marks in 18N.2.HL.TZ0.1: one for the relative uncertainty in ΔT, one for multiplying by ΔH. The part's original command term is not in the pack.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not rework mcΔT at the extremes of the temperature range, and do not revisit the limiting reagent once ΔH is known.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 1 gives Q = mcΔT, showing that Q scales with ΔT. Uncertainty rules and ΔH = −Q/n are NOT in the booklet sections provided and must be memorised.

rules: A percentage alone cannot be an absolute uncertainty in ΔH.
±0.2 kJ just copies the temperature figure across, so it is wrong unless ΔH happens to be numerically equal to ΔT.
With a small percentage on ΔT, a ± close to or above ΔH is wrong. This check fails if ΔT itself is very small, so its percentage uncertainty is large.

evidence.note: Supplies the reaction, the amounts and the 7.5 °C rise. The wording of part (b)(iii) is not in the pack; the ±0.2 °C comes from the markscheme and examiner report.
Part b.iii gives two ticks: 0.2/7.5 as 3% or 0.03, then 0.03 × 160 kJ = ±5 kJ. Part b.i gives ΔH = −1.6 × 10² kJ.
Many earned one mark for the relative uncertainty but did not then multiply by their molar enthalpy.
2025-era evidence: percentage uncertainty in ΔT found by dividing ±2 °C by the change 33−22, with a range of answers accepted.
Calculating the percentage error in heat absorbed by water was poorly done and needs more practice.

cards.difficulty_signal: No % correct in the pack. 18N.2.HL.TZ0.1 examiners report many stopping after one mark, and November 2018 calorimetry calculations are listed as difficult. 25N.1B.HL.6220.2 shows the percentage step in a 2025 paper.
